questions.stem: Why is the ten-year-old Jane locked in the red-room at Gateshead?
options: She runs away and is found hiding in the garden after dark
She fights back after her cousin John Reed throws a book at her
She is caught taking a book from her late uncle's private study
She refuses to apologise to Mrs Reed in front of the visitors
questions.explanation: John Reed bullies Jane and throws a book at her head, and she fights back. She is the one punished, which shows how powerless she is in the Reed household.

questions.stem: What does Mr Brocklehurst do to Jane in front of the whole school at Lowood?
options: Sends her to eat alone and forbids the girls to speak to her
Takes away her books and orders her to scrub the schoolroom
Makes her stand on a stool and tells the girls she is a liar
Cuts off her hair and makes her wear it pinned to her dress
questions.explanation: Brocklehurst repeats Mrs Reed's claim that Jane is deceitful. Jane is shamed in public, and only Helen's kindness and Miss Temple's help get her through it.

questions.stem: What happens at Lowood in the spring of Jane's first year there?
options: Fire destroys the school, and Miss Temple leaves to marry a clergyman
Mr Brocklehurst dies of typhus, and Miss Temple takes charge of the school
Helen dies of typhus, and Jane is sent away from Lowood to recover
Typhus spreads through the school, and Helen dies of consumption
questions.explanation: Cold, hunger and damp let typhus kill many pupils. Helen dies of consumption, not typhus, with Jane sleeping beside her, and the scandal leads to the school being reformed.

questions.stem: How does Jane first meet Mr Rochester?
options: His horse slips on ice in a lane, and she helps him after his fall
He interviews her for the post of governess at an inn in Millcote
She finds him reading in the library when she arrives at Thornfield
He rescues her when she is lost on the moor during a snowstorm
questions.explanation: Jane is walking to post a letter when Rochester's horse slips and he falls. Neither knows the other, and the meeting is unconventional: the poor governess helps the master.

questions.stem: What does Jane do on the night she smells smoke at Thornfield?
options: Follows Grace Poole to the attic and locks her in the room
Runs to the stables and sends the groom for help from the village
Finds Rochester's bed on fire and puts it out with water
Carries Adèle downstairs and rings the bell to wake the servants
questions.explanation: Jane drenches the burning bed and wakes Rochester. He blames Grace Poole and asks Jane to keep quiet, which deepens both the mystery and their closeness.

questions.stem: Why does Jane go back to Gateshead while she is working at Thornfield?
options: Bessie is gravely ill and asks Jane to come and nurse her at the lodge
Bessie writes that Jane's uncle is waiting there to take her abroad
Eliza Reed asks Jane to help settle her late uncle's estate
Mrs Reed is dying and asks to see her, and confesses a lie about Jane
questions.explanation: On her deathbed Mrs Reed admits she told Jane's uncle, John Eyre, that Jane had died at Lowood. She kept Jane from a fortune and a family, and she still cannot forgive her.

questions.stem: What stops Jane's wedding to Rochester?
options: Rochester's horse throws him on the way to church and he is badly hurt
St John Rivers arrives with news that Jane's uncle has forbidden it
Blanche Ingram claims at the altar that Rochester promised to marry her
A solicitor and Richard Mason declare that Rochester is already married
questions.explanation: Mr Briggs and Mason reveal that Rochester's wife, Bertha, is alive. Rochester takes everyone to the third storey, where she has been kept locked away.

questions.stem: After the wedding is stopped, why does Jane leave Thornfield secretly at dawn?
options: She now doubts that Rochester's love for her was ever sincere
She refuses to live with Rochester unmarried, though she loves him
She is afraid that Bertha will escape and try to harm her as well
She has received a letter calling her to her uncle's side in Madeira
questions.explanation: Rochester begs her to live with him abroad as if married. Jane loves him but will not give up her principles or self-respect, so she leaves with almost nothing.

questions.stem: What discovery at Moor House changes Jane's place in the world?
options: Her uncle has left his fortune to St John, who is no relation
Her father was a rich clergyman, and Moor House belongs to her
Her uncle has left her a fortune, and the Rivers are her cousins
Mrs Reed has left her some money, and the Rivers are her Reed cousins
questions.explanation: John Eyre dies and leaves Jane twenty thousand pounds. She learns St John, Diana and Mary are her cousins and shares the money equally with them, gaining both wealth and family.

questions.stem: What does St John Rivers ask of Jane?
options: To go with him to India as his sister and fellow worker
To marry him and work beside him as a missionary in India
To give him her fortune to build a new school at Morton
To stay at Moor House and look after Diana and Mary for him
questions.explanation: St John wants a wife who will be useful in his mission, not one he loves. Jane offers to go as his sister, but he insists on marriage, and she refuses.

questions.stem: What has happened at Thornfield when Jane returns?
options: Bertha has burnt it down, and Rochester died trying to save her
Bertha has burnt it down, and Rochester was blinded and maimed in the fire
Rochester has sold it and married Blanche Ingram, and they live abroad
Grace Poole has burnt it down in a drunken fit, and Bertha has fled to Jamaica
questions.explanation: Bertha set the house alight and died falling from the roof. Rochester tried to save her and lost his sight and one hand, and now lives at Ferndean.

questions.stem: Which list gives the places of Jane's life in the order the novel follows?
options: Gateshead, Lowood, Thornfield, Moor House, Ferndean
Lowood, Gateshead, Thornfield, Ferndean, Moor House
Gateshead, Thornfield, Lowood, Moor House, Ferndean
Lowood, Thornfield, Gateshead, Moor House, Ferndean
questions.explanation: Each place is a stage in Jane's growth: an unloved child, a pupil and teacher, a governess in love, an independent woman and finally a wife. The structure follows a bildungsroman, a story of growing up.

questions.stem: How does Helen Burns's response to injustice differ from Jane's?
options: Helen hates Mr Brocklehurst openly, while Jane hides her anger from him
Helen trusts Mrs Reed's account, while Jane believes she has been lied about
Helen teaches patient endurance and forgiveness, while Jane wants to resist
Helen plans to run away from Lowood, while Jane chooses to stay and obey
questions.explanation: Helen accepts punishment and believes in forgiving wrongs. Jane admires her but cannot share her calm, and the novel weighs both responses rather than simply choosing Helen's.

questions.stem: Who is Miss Temple?
options: The Lowood pupil who befriends Jane and dies of consumption
The kind superintendent of Lowood, who clears Jane's name
The housekeeper at Thornfield, who first welcomes Jane there
The cruel teacher at Lowood, who beats Helen in front of Jane
questions.explanation: Miss Temple writes to Mr Lloyd, who confirms Jane's story, and she clears Jane in front of the school. She is the first adult to treat Jane with fairness and warmth.

questions.stem: St John Rivers is best described as:
options: a hypocritical clergyman who preaches what he does not practise
a warm, humble curate content with a quiet English parish
a cold, ambitious clergyman who puts duty above love
a passionate clergyman who gives up his mission for love
questions.explanation: St John is good and self-sacrificing but icy and controlling. He gives up Rosamond Oliver, whom he loves, because she would not suit a missionary's life.

questions.stem: How do Jane's two suitors, Rochester and St John, act as a contrast?
options: Rochester offers love that would cost her principles, St John duty without love
Rochester offers money without affection, St John affection without money
Rochester offers a life of travel, St John a quiet life in an English village
Rochester offers religious duty, St John a love that is passionate and warm
questions.explanation: Marrying Rochester as things stand would break her principles, and marrying St John would deny her feelings. Jane refuses both until she can have love on terms that keep her integrity.

questions.stem: Who is Bertha Mason?
options: Mrs Fairfax's niece, who works as a maid on the third floor of Thornfield
Adèle's mother, a French singer whom Rochester once hoped to marry
Rochester's wife, whom he married in Jamaica and keeps locked at Thornfield
Rochester's sister, who has come from Jamaica to stop his second marriage
questions.explanation: Rochester married Bertha in Jamaica in a match made for her fortune, and says she later became mad. She is kept in the attic under Grace Poole's watch, and her existence is the secret that stops the wedding.

questions.stem: Who is Adèle Varens?
options: Rochester's young French ward, whom Jane is hired to teach
Rochester's young French cousin, who hopes to marry him herself
Mrs Fairfax's granddaughter, who helps run the household
Rochester's daughter, whom he openly claims as his heir
questions.explanation: Adèle is the daughter of a French dancer, Céline Varens. Rochester took her in although he denies she is his child, and her lessons are why Jane comes to Thornfield.

questions.stem: How was Jane Eyre first published?
options: In 1847, under the pen name Ellis Bell, with a preface
In 1847, under the male-sounding pen name Currer Bell
In 1857, under Charlotte Brontë's own name and title
In 1837, as an anonymous series in a London magazine
questions.explanation: Charlotte and her sisters Emily and Anne used the names Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell. Women writers were often judged more harshly, so a name that could be a man's helped.

questions.stem: Why is a Victorian governess like Jane in an awkward social position?
options: She is forbidden by law to marry while she works in a gentleman's household
She is legally bound to the family until her pupils come of age
She is educated like the family but paid like a servant, so belongs to neither
She is paid more than the family's steward, so the other servants resent her
questions.explanation: A governess was a gentlewoman who had to earn a living. The Ingram party mock governesses in front of Jane, showing how she is seen as neither equal nor servant.

questions.stem: Why is Lowood often linked to Charlotte Brontë's own life?
options: It draws on the school in Brussels where she studied French as an adult
It draws on the school where two of her older sisters fell fatally ill
It draws on the school she founded with her sisters after leaving home
It draws on the orphanage where she worked as a teacher for many years
questions.explanation: Charlotte attended Cowan Bridge school, where conditions were harsh. Her sisters Maria and Elizabeth became ill there and died, and Helen Burns is often linked to Maria.

questions.stem: Jean Rhys's novel Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) tells Bertha's story from her side. Why have modern readers found this response important?
options: Bertha is shown sympathetically in Jane Eyre, so Rhys chose to rewrite her as a villain
Rhys set out to confirm Rochester's account of his marriage to Bertha
Bertha has almost no voice in Jane Eyre, and is seen only through others' eyes
Bertha tells her own story in Jane Eyre, and Rhys simply expanded it
questions.explanation: Jane first sees Bertha as something she cannot tell is 'beast or human being'. Readers now ask how the novel treats a Creole woman from Jamaica, madness and Rochester's account of her.

questions.stem: Which idea is most central to Jane Eyre?
options: The triumph of religious duty over earthly love and personal desire
The strength of family loyalty, which matters more than love or principle
A woman's search for love without giving up her independence and self-respect
The rewards that come to those who accept their place in the social order
questions.explanation: Jane wants love and belonging but refuses any version of them that would make her less than herself. Every major choice she makes tests that balance.

questions.stem: Why does it matter that Jane inherits money before she returns to Rochester?
options: She can pay off Rochester's debts and save Thornfield from his creditors
She can prove to St John that she does not need him or his mission
She can buy Ferndean and give Rochester a home after the fire
She can return as an independent equal, not as a poor dependent
questions.explanation: Jane tells Rochester she is 'an independent woman now'. Money, family and Rochester's new dependence on her mean they marry on far more equal terms than before.

questions.stem: The novel presents three versions of religion through Brocklehurst, Helen and St John. Which best describes them?
options: Stern duty, cheerful doubt, and quiet hypocrisy about wealth
Forgiving faith, ambitious duty, and gentle and loving charity
Hypocrisy, patient and forgiving faith, and stern ambitious duty
Patient faith, cold hypocrisy, and a warm and joyful spirit of forgiveness
questions.explanation: Brocklehurst preaches self-denial to the girls while his own family lives in luxury. Helen's faith is gentle, and St John's is admirable but cold, so Jane must find a faith of her own.

questions.stem: How does the novel treat social class?
options: It upholds the Ingrams' rank as the natural order of society
It questions a society that judges worth by birth and money, not by character
It suggests that marrying up is the proper reward for a virtuous woman
It argues that people should stay in the class into which they were born
questions.explanation: Jane is treated as inferior at Gateshead and by the Ingrams. Her speech claiming equality of soul with Rochester insists that worth lies in the spirit, not in rank.

questions.stem: Who narrates Jane Eyre?
options: Jane, recording events in her diary on the day they happen
Jane, looking back as an adult who has been married ten years
Rochester, telling the story of the governess who saved him
An omniscient narrator who moves between the characters' minds
questions.explanation: The novel is a first-person retrospective. The adult Jane tells us 'I have now been married ten years', so she judges her younger self while letting us feel her experience.

questions.stem: Jane often speaks straight to 'Reader'. What is the effect?
options: It creates distance, reminding us that the story is a fiction
It creates suspense, by hiding what Jane really thinks about events
It creates irony, showing that Jane's account cannot be trusted
It creates intimacy, as if Jane is confiding in the reader as a friend
questions.explanation: Direct address draws us into Jane's confidence and makes her account feel like testimony. The most famous example is 'Reader, I married him.'

questions.stem: Which features of the Thornfield chapters belong to Gothic fiction?
options: An orphan's schooling, harsh discipline and growth into adulthood
A clergyman's proposal, missionary duty and a call to serve in India
A dark secret in the attic, a strange laugh at night and a mysterious fire
A plain governess, a proud wealthy master and a love that crosses class lines
questions.explanation: Brontë uses Gothic conventions: a mansion hiding a secret, eerie sounds and danger at night. They build suspense and make Jane's love story strange and threatening.

questions.stem: On the night of the proposal, the great horse-chestnut in the orchard is struck by lightning and split. What does this suggest?
options: That the coming marriage is doomed and the lovers will be torn apart
That nature blesses their marriage with a sign of its power
That Rochester's house will soon be struck by lightning and burn down
That Jane and Rochester will grow old together, side by side, like the tree
questions.explanation: The proposal happens under the tree, and the storm breaks that night. The split trunk foreshadows the broken wedding and the separation that follows.

questions.stem: The night before she leaves Thornfield, Jane dreams she is back in the red-room at Gateshead. Why is this effective?
options: It hints that Jane will return to Gateshead to live with the Reeds again
It links her first rebellion as a child to her new crisis of feeling trapped
It reveals that the red-room was where Bertha was kept before her marriage
It shows that Jane has forgotten Gateshead and no longer fears the past
questions.explanation: The red-room stands for being imprisoned and powerless. Recalling it as she decides to leave shows the adult Jane once again facing confinement, this time choosing her own escape.

questions.stem: Who says 'I am no bird; and no net ensnares me'?
options: Jane, to Rochester in the orchard before he proposes
Jane, to St John when he asks her to go to India
Jane, to Rochester as she leaves Thornfield at dawn
Helen, to Jane in the garden at Lowood before she dies
questions.explanation: Rochester calls Jane a 'wild frantic bird' and she answers that she is a free human being with an independent will. It is a declaration of her freedom and equality.

questions.stem: Jane asks Rochester, 'Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless?' What is she claiming?
options: That she is too poor and plain to be a suitable wife for a gentleman
That she has hidden her real feelings from him because of her position
That she wants him to give her money and status before she will marry
That her soul and feelings are equal to his, whatever her rank or looks
questions.explanation: She goes on to say she has 'as much soul' and 'full as much heart' as he does. The speech claims spiritual equality across class and gender.

questions.stem: What does Jane's narration 'women feel just as men feel' argue?
options: That women's feelings suit them better for love than for work
That women need action and a field for their efforts, just as men do
That women should hide their feelings in order to be good wives
That women should be content with needlework and other domestic duties
questions.explanation: Restless at Thornfield, Jane says women suffer from 'too rigid a restraint'. The passage is one of the novel's clearest statements about the limits placed on women.

questions.stem: Helen Burns says, 'Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity or registering wrongs.' What does this show?
options: Her belief in forgiveness, which Jane finds admirable but hard to share
Her bitterness at Lowood, which she hides from the teachers and Jane
Her wish to leave school soon and see more of the world before she dies
Her anger at Mrs Reed, whom she blames for Jane's unhappy childhood
questions.explanation: Helen tells this to Jane, who is full of resentment against Mrs Reed. Her patient faith gives Jane a model of self-control she slowly learns from.

questions.stem: When Jane says, 'The more solitary, the more friendless, the more unsustained I am, the more I will respect myself,' what is she deciding?
options: To refuse St John because she would be lonely in his mission
To stay at Lowood as a teacher rather than face the world alone
To leave Moor House rather than live on the Rivers' charity
To leave Rochester rather than give up her principles for him
questions.explanation: Rochester pleads that no one would be harmed if she stayed. Jane holds to her principles because she is alone and tempted: 'Laws and principles are not for the times when there is no temptation'.

questions.stem: Who says 'God and nature intended you for a missionary's wife', and what does it reveal?
options: Rochester, who mocks Jane for being too serious and religious for him
Mr Brocklehurst, who wants Jane to leave Lowood and go to India
Diana Rivers, who hopes Jane will marry her brother and stay near her
St John, who sees Jane as useful for his mission rather than loving her
questions.explanation: St John proposes as if Jane's life were a job he has chosen for her. His certainty that he knows God's will makes his proposal hard to resist and coldly controlling.

questions.stem: 'Reader, I married him.' What is notable about the wording of this line?
options: Jane speaks of Rochester by name for the first time in the book
Jane addresses Rochester directly instead of the reader
Jane announces the wedding before the proposal has happened
Jane is the subject of the sentence: she does the marrying
questions.explanation: Jane does not say 'he married me'. The sentence makes her the active one, matching her claim to choose her life on her own terms.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'Jane Eyre is a novel about a woman who refuses to be owned.' Discuss.
options: Jane Eyre is a novel by Charlotte Brontë that was published in 1847 as Currer Bell
This essay will discuss how Jane is shown as a woman in the novel Jane Eyre
In Jane Eyre, Jane is an orphan who goes to Lowood and then to Thornfield Hall
Brontë shows Jane resisting every attempt to control her, from John Reed to St John
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence names the author, takes a position on the prompt and points to what the paragraph will prove. The others announce, retell or give facts without an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Jane leaves Thornfield early in the morning with very little money.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Explain how leaving with nothing shows she values self-respect above comfort
Add the exact amount of money Jane has and the name of the coach driver
List the other things Jane leaves behind in her room at Thornfield Hall
Describe each place Jane passes through on her journey to Whitcross
questions.explanation: Analysis says what the evidence shows. Linking Jane's poverty on leaving to her refusal to compromise connects the event to the novel's ideas about independence.
